lesson.title: Ask a question, then collect
lesson.subtitle: Plan the sheet, collect only what you need, save it to share

video.title: Ask a question, then collect
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Okafor — science teacher, Nigeria, runs the weather club (main character)
Mr Joseph — computer studies teacher, Kenya (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: Icon cards: A month; Which week?; “a lot”, “12”. Mr Okafor beside it.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Our weather club measured rain for a whole month. Then I asked: which week was the wettest? The sheet said “a lot”, “12”, “12 mm” and “heavy”, and the dates were written three different ways!

scenes.visual: Paper-grey title card: the Darsi mark, the course name and the lesson title with the Data engineering track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark scales in with a small overshoot; the title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: start with a question, then collect data that can answer it.

scenes.visual: Rows of icon and text: Which week was wettest?; How long is the walk?; Collect what answers it; Skip what doesn't.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Good data starts with a question. Which week had the most rain? How long do pupils walk to school? The question tells you what to collect, and just as important, what not to collect.

scenes.visual: Numbered steps: One column per fact; The unit in the heading: Rain (mm); Fixed codes: P, A, L; Dates one way: 2026-03-02.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Then plan the sheet before anyone writes a thing. One column per fact, with the unit in the heading, like rain in millimetres. Fixed codes, like P, A and L for present, absent and late. And every date written the same way.

scenes.visual: Icon cards joined by arrows: Tally on paper; Count the fives; Type into a sheet.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: On paper, tally marks are the quickest way to count: four strokes, then a fifth across them. Later, type the counts into a spreadsheet, one row at a time.

scenes.visual: Code typed out on a card: date,class,pupil,status … Caption: One line per row, commas between the values
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.on_screen_text: CSV: a table as plain text
scenes.narration: Most spreadsheets can save a file as CSV, comma-separated values. It's plain text: one line per row, with commas between the values, and the column names on the first line. Any program can open it, today or in twenty years.

scenes.visual: Rows of icon and text: Arabic names in the sheet; Save as “CSV UTF-8”; Otherwise: garbled letters. Mr Joseph beside it.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: One tip from the computer room. When your sheet has Arabic names, save it as CSV UTF-8. Otherwise the letters can arrive as nonsense on someone else's computer.

scenes.visual: Quiz card: the question with its answer options.
scenes.animation: Answer cards drop in one by one.
scenes.narration: Quick check! Our club wants to know which week this term had the most rain. Which data does that question really need?

scenes.visual: Icon cards: The date; Rain (mm); Not names or photos; Less is safer.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: The date and the rain in millimetres: that's all the question needs. Names and photos don't help it, so don't collect them. Less data is quicker to collect, easier to check, and safer to keep.

scenes.visual: Two columns: “JSON” (Repeats every column name; Nearly 5 minutes on 2G) and “Compressed” (Repeats squeezed out; About 13 seconds).
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: How you save data also decides what it costs to send. The same attendance as JSON repeats every column name in every record, so it's more than twice the size of CSV. On a slow 2G connection, a school's term of it takes nearly five minutes; compressed, about thirteen seconds.

scenes.visual: Icon cards joined by arrows: How much data; Which format; Which network; Time to download.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.on_screen_text: App lab: same data, different sizes
scenes.narration: In the app, choose how much data, the format and the network. See the file's size and how long it takes to download. How would you send your school's term?

scenes.visual: Quiz card: the question with its answer options.
scenes.animation: Answer cards drop in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. Our club wrote “twelve”, “twelve mm” and “a lot” for the same kind of day. What would have stopped that?

scenes.visual: Summary card: Question first; Plan: units, codes, dates; Only what you need; CSV opens anywhere. Takeaway bar: A good question saves you from collecting the wrong data.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: A planned sheet, with the unit in the heading and numbers only, would have stopped it. Remember: start from a question. Plan the sheet before you collect. Collect only what you need. And save it in a format others can open and afford to send.

scenes.visual: Rows of icon and text: One question; Agree columns, units, codes; Tally on paper; Type it, save as CSV. Mr Okafor beside it.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: ask your pupils one question, like how long it takes them to get to school. Agree on the columns, the units and the codes together. Collect the answers with tally marks, then type them into a sheet and save it as CSV.

checkpoints.prompt: Your weather club asks: which week this term had the most rain? Which data does that question need?

options.text: The date and the rain in mm each day
The names and ages of the club members
A photo of the sky each day

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — the date and the rain in mm answer the question. Anything else is extra work and extra risk.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — the question is about rain in each week, so you need the date and the rain in mm. Names and photos don't answer it.

checkpoints.prompt: Readings came in as “12”, “12 mm” and “a lot”. What would have stopped that?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — with the unit in the heading, everyone writes just the number, and the computer can add them up.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — the problem was no plan: put the unit in the heading and write numbers only.
